title: "We Only Protect What We Love"
author: Beanie Geoghegan
summary: Beanie Geoghegan asks whether American public schools give students enough understanding to love, and therefore protect, their country, borrowing Jacques Cousteau's line that "we only protect what we love, we only love what we understand, and we only understand what we are taught." She rejects the idea that most teachers are indoctrinating students against America, citing an Education Next survey in which 57 percent of the youngest teachers say it is important to teach that America is fundamentally good. The real problem, she argues, is structural: social studies has absorbed history, civics, economics and geography, standards have swapped explicit knowledge for vague "21st-century skills," and instructional time has shrunk. Her remedies are more class time, which she says Louisiana is securing through annual social studies assessments in grades 3, 5 and 8, standards built on clear sequential content, and high-quality curriculum such as Hillsdale and Core Knowledge. She closes by treating events in France as a canary in the coal mine for what happens when a country does not teach its own history.
points: The piece frames civic loyalty as a knowledge problem: students cannot love or defend what they were never taught to understand.
Geoghegan locates the failure in structure, namely merged social studies, skills-first standards and lost class time, instead of in teacher ideology.
Louisiana's plan to assess social studies in grades 3, 5 and 8 is offered as a model because assessed subjects receive the most instructional time.
State standards should move from vague skills to clear, sequential, content-specific expectations, as in Florida, Texas and Louisiana.
Content-rich curricula such as Hillsdale's K-12 history and civics and Core Knowledge are recommended, especially for K-5 teachers who must teach every subject.
quotes: Many state social studies standards have replaced explicit knowledge of key people, events, and dates with vague “21st-century skills.” Classroom time dedicated to teaching social studies has also significantly dwindled.
In reality, according to an Education Next survey, 57 percent of the youngest teachers surveyed say it is important to teach that America is fundamentally good.
That is the unifying identity every public school student in America can claim.
That requires adequate instructional time, content-focused standards, and excellent, high-quality instructional resources for teachers.
One thing No Child Left Behind made clear is that assessed subjects receive the most instructional time.
To maximize the effectiveness of class time, states must revise their standards and shift from vague, subjective skills to clear, sequential content.
Sadly, many teachers rely on unvetted, inferior online resources because their districts have not provided alternatives.
Future generations must know about and love America enough to protect it unapologetically and without hesitation.
